title: A method for estimating width bands of variables in economics under uncertainty conditions
author: Ganjoei, Akbarifard, et al.

steps.title: Set up software and data
steps.instruction: Install and launch EViews (for LSTAR modeling) and MATLAB (for fuzzy inference). Load the time‑series dataset containing the variables OPEN (degree of economic openness), FDI (foreign direct investment), IIT (integration of international trade) and Gini coefficient (Ginit) for the period 1997‑2017.

steps.title: Test stationarity with ADF
steps.instruction: In EViews run the Augmented Dickey‑Fuller (ADF) unit‑root test on each variable. Estimate the regression ΔYt = (ρ‑1)Yt‑1 + ut = δYt‑1 + ut, where Δ denotes first difference. Test the null hypothesis H0: δ = 0 (unit root, non‑stationary) using the special ADF t‑statistic table.

steps.title: Test linearity and perform LM tests
steps.instruction: Test the linear model against a nonlinear alternative. Use the null hypothesis H0: v = 0 (linear) where the transition function G(st;v,c) = (1+exp{‑v(st‑c)})⁻¹, v>0. Replace the transition function by its third‑order Taylor expansion around v = 0 to obtain the auxiliary regression (Eq. 15). Compute the Lagrange‑Multiplier (LM) statistic LMW = T·(SSR0‑SSR1)/SSR0:

substeps.instruction: Regress yt on xt and obtain SSR0 = Σt=1^T σ̂_t² (σ̂ is the residual variance).
Regress the residuals σ̂_t on xt and the nonlinear regressors of Eq. 16, obtain SSR1 = Σt=1^T τ̂_t².
Calculate LMW and compare to its critical values. The LM null hypothesis is H0: β1′ = β2′ = β3′ = 0.

steps.title: Determine optimal lag order
steps.instruction: Compute Akaike (AIC), Bayesian (BIC) and Hannan‑Quinn (HQ) information criteria for lag lengths 0‑3 and select the lag with the lowest values. The table of results is:

substeps.instruction: Lag 1: AIC ‑4.718*, BIC ‑4.834*, HQ ‑5.230* (optimal lag = 1)

steps.title: Specify Taylor approximations for variables
steps.instruction: Write the first‑, second‑ and third‑order Taylor series for each explanatory variable as follows (β coefficients are to be estimated):

substeps.instruction: FDI (Eqs 17‑19):
(17) Ginit = β01 + β02 Ginit‑1 + β03 FDI‑1 + β04 OPEN‑1 + β05 IIT‑1 + β11(FDI‑1·Ginit‑1) + β12(FDI‑1²) + β13(FDI‑1·OPEN‑1) + β14(FDI‑1·IIT‑1) + εt
(18) add second‑order terms β21(Ginit‑1·FDI‑1²) + β22(FDI‑1³) + β23(OPEN‑1·FDI‑1²) + β24(IIT‑1·FDI‑1²)
(19) add third‑order terms β31(Ginit‑1·FDI‑1³) + β32(FDI‑1⁴) + β33(FDI‑1³·OPEN‑1) + β34(FDI‑1³·IIT‑1)
OPEN (Eqs 20‑22): analogous expressions with OPEN‑1 interacting with Ginit‑1, FDI‑1, IIT‑1 and higher‑order terms.
IIT (Eqs 23‑25): analogous expressions with IIT‑1 interacting with Ginit‑1, FDI‑1, OPEN‑1 and higher‑order terms.
Gini with one lag (Eqs 26‑28): analogous expressions with Ginit‑1 interacting with FDI‑1, OPEN‑1, IIT‑1 and higher‑order terms.

steps.title: Select transition variable
steps.instruction: For each independent variable (OPEN, FDI, IIT, Ginit‑1) compute the LMW statistic defined above. Choose the variable with the highest LMW value as the transition (transfer) variable for the LSTAR model.

steps.title: Choose transition function via hypothesis testing
steps.instruction: Test the following nested hypotheses in order:

substeps.instruction: H1: β3′ = 0 → if rejected, adopt LSTAR form.
If H1 accepted, test H2: β2′ = 0 | β3′ = 0 → if rejected, adopt ESTAR form.
If H2 accepted, test H3: β1′ = 0 | β2′ = 0, β3′ = 0 → if rejected, adopt LSTAR; otherwise model is linear.

steps.title: Estimate transition parameters v and c
steps.instruction: Use the Newton‑Raphson algorithm to solve for the transition velocity v and transition point c in the logistic function. Initialise v and c with the approximations given in Eq. 29 and iterate until convergence:

substeps.instruction: Eq. 29: Gini = α0 + α1 Ginit‑1 + α2 FDI‑1 + α3 IIT‑1 + α4 OPEN‑1 + (β0+β1 Ginit‑1+β2 FDI‑1+β3 IIT‑1+β4 OPEN‑1)·(1+exp{‑v(OPEN‑1‑c)})⁻¹ + εt
Iterate Newton‑Raphson on v and c using the partial derivatives of the likelihood with respect to v and c.

steps.title: Compute threshold values of transition function
steps.instruction: Calculate the logistic transition function values using G(st;v,c) = (1+exp{‑v(st‑c)})⁻¹, with v>0, for the selected transition variable st. These values serve as the thresholds between regimes in the LSTAR model.

steps.title: Build fuzzy inference system in MATLAB
steps.instruction: Create a Mamdani fuzzy inference system (FIS) for estimating Gini bands.

substeps.instruction: Enter the fuzzy environment by typing the command fuzzy in MATLAB; the FIS editor appears.
Define four input membership functions (Gaussian) for FDI, IIT, OPEN and Gini‑t‑1: μA(x)=exp[‑(x‑c)²/(2σ²)], where c is the mean and σ the standard deviation.
Define one output membership function (Gaussian) for the Gini coefficient (see Appendix for parameters).

Construct the rule base: compute the number of rules I = mⁿ, where m = number of linguistic terms (e.g., High, Middle, Low) and n = 4 inputs. Populate the rules as in Table 2 (e.g., IF FDI is High AND IIT is High AND OPEN is High AND Gini‑t‑1 is Low THEN Gini is High, etc.).
Set the inference engine to Mamdani type.
Choose the centroid defuzzification method: output = ∫ x·μ(x) dx / ∫ μ(x) dx.

steps.title: Estimate Gini coefficient bands with fuzzy rules
steps.instruction: Apply the fuzzy‑rule base to the data to obtain fuzzified inputs and compute the estimated Gini for three width bands (N = 3) using Eq. 30:

substeps.instruction: G̃_i,t = Σ_{j=1}^n α_j G̃_{t‑j} + Σ_{j=1}^n α_j FDĨ_{t‑j} + Σ_{j=1}^n α_j OPEÑ_{t‑j} + Σ_{j=1}^n α_j IIT̃_{t‑j} + G̃(S̃_{it}, ṽ, c̃)·{same sum}
Use i = 1,2,3 (high, middle, low bands), t = 1,…,T (T = 2017), j = 1,…,n (n = 20, years 1997‑2017). All variables are fuzzified (denoted by ~).
